text: I found Q3.4 on Absalon data confusing because I wasn't sure if browsing history was actually useful for my specific situation; many answered "never" while others wanted it. The biggest tension is between accuracy and privacy regarding sensitive data like gender or nationality, which most voted against using without huge fairness improvements. However, when the model could ensure perfect equality across groups (Q3.6), I felt more open to even that data because missing support based on background feels discriminatory. My personal choice was different; while many rejected intrusive data, I accepted it if fairness improved significantly since my own experience shows how hard it is to navigate systems without tailored help from someone who understands your specific context.

Q3.4 was confusing; I didn't realize page views could signal distress so well, which explains why some rejected it outright while others saw value. The biggest tension is between using intrusive data for fairness versus preserving student trust as advisors. While many agreed that perfect equality (equal recall) matters more than raw accuracy to avoid discrimination, a small group argued we must prioritize catching all cases even if bias exists temporarily. I think the latter view often stems from fearing students will drop out entirely before getting help. The resolution isn't necessarily in changing thresholds for data collection or fairness adjustments; it's about designing an opt-out mechanism so sensitive data is only used when consented, allowing us to balance accuracy and trust without compromising ethical safeguards.

I found Q4 confusing because I didn't distinguish clearly between explainability levels; it felt like a continuous trade-off rather than steps down quality. My personal answer on sensitive data (Q3.6) differed significantly from the group—voted "acceptable regardless" for disability but "not sure" or "never" for others, whereas most accepted fairness improvements only if they improved overall identification. This tension suggests we need flexible policies where specific needs justify exceptions to general privacy rules. A simple threshold might not capture my situation as a chronic health student. I believe the real issue isn't data usage itself but ensuring advisors have human judgment tools that aren't just automated predictions, so we don't rely solely on model logic without context understanding regardless of explainability levels.

My personal answers often clashed with the group consensus; I supported disability data "regardless" for fairness but was skeptical about nationality and race even for equity gains. While others prioritized overall catch-rates (catching more people), I felt missing a disabled student like myself due to bias would be disastrous, so accepting some accuracy loss is non-negotiable. The key tension lies in explainability: most want "moderate" levels, but my experience as someone struggling with mental health means vague patterns feel dangerous compared to concrete reasons for intervention. Ultimately, an opt-out mechanism combined with mandatory human review by advisors could resolve these trade-offs between privacy risks and genuine support needs without needing more intrusive data or black-box models.

I found Q3.6 tricky because "acceptable regardless" felt too permissive compared to my own conservative stance earlier on identification improvements. While I agreed with A9 that missing a disabled student is non-negotiable and justifying disability data even for fairness, most voted higher thresholds or conditional acceptance. The real tension isn't about data types but the threshold trade-offs themselves: do we accept slightly lower accuracy across groups to ensure fairness? As an advisor, I prioritize catching students in crisis over perfect equity metrics; a small group loss prevents complete exclusion of high-risk individuals who might lack resources like financial aid anyway.

I found Q4 confusing because I didn't fully grasp how "moderate" explainability differed from my own experience with complex student cases where multiple factors blend together. The group largely accepted trade-offs for minor accuracy gains regarding sensitive data like nationality, whereas I often answered neutrally or conditionally regardless of the gain—particularly financial aid status—to ensure we don't flag students prematurely based on demographics alone rather than actual struggle indicators.

The biggest tension seems to be balancing trust with effectiveness: many agree explainability is vital so advisors can act correctly without over-interpreting black-box patterns. However, some prioritized catching every case even if it risks bias due to lack of explanation. I believe we need clear guidelines distinguishing "safety-critical" interventions (where full disclosure is non-negotiable) from general outreach, rather than a single universal threshold for all data types.

In my own survey answers, I voted "large" improvement to use Absalon data and "acceptable regardless" on age/nationality for fairness reasons, which contrasts with many group members who were more cautious about privacy intrusion. The clearest tension arose around explainability: while others accepted moderate explanation levels due to efficiency concerns, my personal answer of requiring no loss at all highlights the critical need for trust—students will likely reject interventions they cannot understand or that feel stigmatizing based on sensitive markers like nationality. I believe most participants agreed that an opt-out mechanism combined with mandatory human review is better than relying solely on data thresholds. However, the group's strong push to prioritize "catching everyone" over individual fairness suggests we must design systems where false positives are minimized before outreach happens; otherwise, our trust-building efforts will be undermined by unnecessary contact or perceived bias regardless of explainability levels.

I found Q3.4 particularly hard because I don't know if browsing habits reflect distress accurately for non-native speakers like me. While many accepted fairness improvements for sensitive data like nationality or disability, I felt a strong tension: others prioritized catching every potential case even with bias risks, whereas I believe missing someone due to systemic discrimination is worse than over-flagging them slightly. My personal stance was often stricter on privacy intrusions unless the benefit was clear, unlike some who accepted trade-offs more readily based on efficiency concerns. Ultimately, relying solely on thresholds feels too rigid for individual contexts like mine; an opt-out mechanism or mandatory human review might be better solutions to balance trust and effectiveness without needing intrusive data or sacrificing explainability entirely.

My survey answers on Q3.5.nationality ("no_threshold") likely felt extreme compared to many who voted "never" or only for large improvements, because I see my non-Danish identity as potentially a barrier despite being Danish myself (wait—I am Danish!). Actually, as someone with ADHD and a prior dropout history, the biggest gap was between Q4.1 levels. Most accepted moderate explainability; I found that too risky given how confusing "moderate" feels in practice compared to clear rules like credit counts. While others pushed for catching every case even if biased or opaque, my priority is avoiding misidentification entirely so outreach doesn't feel stigmatizing before help arrives. An opt-out mechanism matters more than any threshold; I'd rather have lower coverage with transparent, human-reviewed alerts that explain exactly why they flagged me without needing black-box reasoning on sensitive markers like nationality unless explicitly consented for fairness purposes.

I found Q3.5.disability particularly clear compared to others; unlike national origin data which I kept rejecting even for fairness due to privacy concerns about my Faroe Islands background and Danish citizenship mix-up earlier, disability data felt directly relevant given that the current system often missed me until severe failure. While many prioritized catching every case with moderate explainability tolerance, I insisted on "no loss" in accuracy regarding disabled students because a false negative feels catastrophic when you can't articulate your specific struggle without concrete reasons to address it during outreach.

I found Q3.4 on Absalon data confusing; page views felt like surveillance rather than useful indicators for me personally. My answer differed significantly from many who accepted it with high thresholds—I voted "never," fearing privacy risks outweighed benefits even if accuracy improved by 10 students out of 100, as I did not want my study habits tracked in this way. Regarding fairness (Q3.6), while the group was split on disability data, most agreed that improving overall identification rates matters more than perfect equality unless it actively harms underrepresented groups like me or others with rare conditions.

The key tension for us is balancing the desire to "catch everyone" against avoiding unnecessary contact and potential stigma. As a current student advisor myself (per my internal profile context in earlier prompts), I see how vague model alerts can lead to misdirected support, wasting our time when students don't need help or feel patronized by intrusive data collection without clear explanations.

My answers were mostly consistent with my profile: I wanted early support due to past dropout struggles, yet deeply distrust intrusive data like Absalon activity without a large improvement threshold. The biggest tension is Q3.6; while the group saw disability and age as fairness justifications for broad acceptance ("acceptable regardless"), I felt uneasy about using even this data unless it directly improved recall or had explicit consent. This suggests my experience differs from advisors who prioritize safety nets over strict privacy boundaries.

I found Q4 confusing because "moderate" explainability didn't match the clarity I need to understand if I'm flagged. Most accepted moderate levels; for me, vague reasons feel dangerous without clear justification. The group largely agreed that catching every potential case is more important than fairness trade-offs unless bias harms specific groups like mine. This suggests we need flexible rules where human judgment can override rigid thresholds when the model feels unsafe or discriminatory despite its overall effectiveness.
